1.title: the one at every doorway
1.hook: an elephant-headed figure on the dashboard, by the door, at the top of the page
1.howItsDone: Hindus honor Ganesha first at ceremonies, weddings and new beginnings, keep his image near doorways and in shops, and some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before starting to write.

segments.voice: Every Hindu beginning starts with him, so this one does too. A small statue on a taxi dashboard. A picture above a shop counter. His name printed at the top of a wedding invitation, before anyone else's. Elephant head, round belly, one tusk broken. He sits wherever things start, and that's the clue to who he is.
screen: `EVERY BEGINNING STARTS WITH HIM.` → `DASHBOARDS. DOORWAYS. INVITATIONS.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Ganesha is gana plus isha: lord of the ganas, the attendants of the god Shiva. But the title that explains the doorways is Vighnaharta. Vighna, an obstacle; harta, one who removes. The remover of obstacles. That's why he's honored first: before a ceremony, a wedding, a new shop or an exam. Some people write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before they begin: namah means a bow. There's a popular way of reading his body: big ears, listen more than you talk; small eyes, focus; a big belly, take in what life serves, good and hard. And the broken tusk: tradition says he wrote down the Mahabharata as the sage Vyasa dictated it, and one story says that when his pen gave out, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing.

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Rest a hand on something that marks a start: a door, a laptop, a notebook. Name, once, what's in the way of the next thing you're beginning. Then breathe out and lift your hand.
Ganesha. Lord of the ganas, remover of obstacles, the one at the door. First word on your strand, and the first name.

2.title: the sound the universe hums
2.hook: the sound a room makes together; it's three sounds and a silence
2.tomorrow: the prayer you know by heart
2.howItsDone: Hindus chant om at the start of prayers, mantras and readings of scripture, often at the end too, and it is written as a single sacred sign, ॐ, in homes and temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesha, the one who goes first. Today, the sound that opens almost every Hindu prayer.

Om. A yoga class ends with it, and a lot of Hindu prayers begin with it. Most people treat it as one long hum. One of the oldest Hindu texts hears four parts in it: three sounds, and a fourth that isn't a sound at all. First, a guess.

Say it slowly and you can feel three sounds. A, with the mouth open. U, as the lips round. M, as they close. That's why it's sometimes written aum. An old text of just twelve verses starts by saying om is all of this: past, present, future, and whatever lies beyond time. Then it maps the sounds onto your day. A is waking, the world you can see and touch. U is dreaming, the world made of the mind. M is deep, dreamless sleep, where nothing is wanted. The fourth part has no sound. It's the silence after the m runs out, and the text calls it simply the fourth: the self, at peace. So om isn't a sign-off. It's a map of a whole day in one breath, with the quiet underneath it. The Bhagavad Gita says acts of offering, giving and discipline begin with it.
screen: `A — WAKING.` · `U — DREAMING.` · `M — DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH — THE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. Let it out as the sound, aloud or under your breath: a, u, m. Let the m run out on its own, then stay a second in the quiet after it. That quiet is the fourth part.
Om. A, u and m for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after it for the fourth. Second word on your strand.

segments.voice: Your line: one sound, before words. Not a task. Something to notice the next time a room goes quiet before it begins. Day two, done.

story.title: the boy who waited for Death
story.text: A boy named Nachiketa is sent to Death by his angry father, and he actually goes. Death isn't home, so the boy waits three days at the door without food. To make up for it, Death offers him three wishes. For the third, Nachiketa asks what happens after we die. Death offers him gold, long life, whole kingdoms, anything else instead. The boy says no. So Death teaches him, and part of the teaching is a single word: om.

3.title: the prayer you know by heart
3.hook: the prayer you can say start to finish, and what it asks for
3.carry: a prayer for a clear mind
3.howItsDone: Many Hindus say the Gayatri mantra at dawn, and often at dusk, sometimes a set number of times on a mala; it opens with om bhur bhuvah svah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: om, three sounds and a silence. Today it opens a prayer you might already know by heart.

Om bhur bhuvah svah. If you grew up in a Hindu home, there's a good chance you can say the rest without thinking. Maybe someone said it every morning. Maybe it played at every puja. Now the hard part: what does it mean? Most people go quiet. Today, line by line. First, a guess.
screen: `OM BHUR BHUVAH SVAH…` → `YOU CAN SAY IT.` → `WHAT DOES IT MEAN?`

segments.voice: It's called the Gayatri mantra, and it's one of the oldest verses Hindus still say every day. Take it a line at a time. Om: the sound from yesterday. Bhur bhuvah svah: earth, sky, and everything beyond: the whole world. Tat savitur varenyam: that bright, worthy light of the sun. Bhargo devasya dhimahi: we meditate on that divine radiance. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may it wake up and guide our minds. Notice what it asks for. Not money. Not luck. Not to win. A clear mind. That's what a mantra is: the word comes from man, to think, and tra, a tool. A tool for the mind, said on purpose. Many families say the Gayatri at dawn, as the light comes up, and some say it a set number of times on beads. Once you know the lines, it stops being a sound you repeat and becomes a request you mean.
screen: `OM — THE SOUND FROM YESTERDAY.` · `EARTH, SKY, AND BEYOND.` · `MAY IT WAKE UP OUR MINDS.` · `A TOOL FOR THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Breathe in. As you breathe out, say the Gayatri once, slowly, out loud or in your head, or just its last line: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, may it wake up and guide our minds. This time, mean the words.
Gayatri. The morning prayer for a clear mind, and a mantra: a tool for the mind. Third word on your strand.
Your line: a prayer for a clear mind. Next time you hear it, you'll know what's being asked. Day three.

4.title: the oldest hello
4.hook: you've said it after yoga class; the words inside say more than hello
4.carry: the light in me sees the light in you
4.howItsDone: Hindus greet one another with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed. The same gesture is made to elders, to guests and before images of the gods.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Gayatri, a prayer for a clear mind. Today, a word you've said a thousand times as hello.

You've said it at the end of a yoga class, and you've probably heard it means the light in me sees the light in you. The word itself says something much simpler. The longer meaning is a reading of it, and that reading comes from somewhere specific. First, a guess.

Namaste is Sanskrit, and it splits in two. Namas: a bow. Te: to you. Word for word, I bow to you. That's the whole dictionary meaning. So where does the light come from? From a reading of the word. One of the oldest Hindu texts describes a light that shines above the heavens, above everything, and then says that same light is the light inside a person. Out there and in here: one light. Put that next to a bow and you get the popular line: the light in me sees the light in you. Not a translation. An interpretation, with a real source behind it. What the reading changes is who you're bowing to. Not someone's job, mood or résumé, but whatever in them is the same as what's in you. And nobody has to earn it first. In this reading, it's already there. The same bow goes further at home. When a kid touches a grandparent's feet at the door, that's pranam, from pra, forward, and nam, to bend: the same root as namaste. And the elder's hand comes down on the child's head: a blessing, given back. Respect goes one way, a blessing comes the other.
screen: `NAMAS — A BOW.` · `TE — TO YOU.` · `THE SAME LIGHT, INSIDE A PERSON.` · `A BLESSING, GIVEN BACK.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Palms together if you like, or just sit up straight. Breathe in. As you breathe out, tip your head slightly forward: the bow the word is named for. Nothing to feel, nothing to get right. Just the gesture, done once, on purpose.
Namaste. Word for word, I bow to you. Read deeper, the light in me sees the light in you. Fourth word on your strand.
Your line: the light in me sees the light in you. Not a task. Just a way to look at the next person you meet. That's day four.

5.title: light passed hand to hand
5.hook: a flame on a plate, moved in circles, then carried around the room
5.howItsDone: Arti is performed in temples and homes, often in the morning and evening: a lamp is waved before the image of God while a bell rings and a song is sung, and then the flame is brought to each person, who passes their hands over it and touches their eyes and forehead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: namaste, I bow to you, and the bow that touches an elder's feet. Today, the flame that comes around on a plate.

Evening at a temple. Or the steps down to a river, as dusk comes in. Or a living room, when the lamp comes out. A small flame sits on a metal plate, and someone moves it in slow circles in front of the shrine. A bell rings. People sing. Then the plate is carried around the room, and one by one, people pass their hands over the flame and bring their palms to their eyes and forehead. It takes a few minutes, start to finish. Today's word is that flame, and what happens when it leaves the shrine.
screen: `A FLAME ON A PLATE.` → `SLOW CIRCLES. A BELL.` → `THEN IT COMES TO THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Arti. The waving of a lamp; the offering of light. After the flowers and food are offered, the lamp is circled before the image of God, and a song is sung. The best known begins: Om jai jagadish hare. Victory to you, lord of the world. An old Hindu text has a line that helps with what the lamp might mean: the sun doesn't shine there, nor the moon and stars, let alone this little fire; everything shines after that one shining. So a small flame held up before God is light offered back to where light comes from. Then the flame leaves the shrine and goes out to the people. Each person draws its warmth toward their face. The same small fire touches every face in the room, and nobody gets more of it. Often there's one more step: prasad. Food or sweets offered before God, then handed out. The sweet you got after temple as a kid was that: an offering, given back as a blessing.
screen: `ARTI — THE OFFERING OF LIGHT` · `EVERYTHING SHINES AFTER THAT ONE` · `THE SAME FIRE TOUCHES EVERY FACE` · `PRASAD — GIVEN BACK AS A BLESSING`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. If there's a candle or a lamp near you, look at it; any light in the room will do. Cup your hands toward it, as if gathering warmth, and bring them to your eyes and forehead. Then bring one person to mind and turn your cupped hands toward them, as if passing the plate.
Arti. The offering of light, and then the light shared with everyone. Fifth word.
Your line: light passed hand to hand. Next time the plate comes around, you'll know what you're doing. Day five.

6.title: why so many gods?
6.hook: why there are so many gods, and which one is yours
6.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep images of several deities; many families have a chosen deity (ishta devata) and a family deity, and devotion ranges from one god held as supreme to many honored together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arti, light passed hand to hand. Today, the question every Hindu kid gets asked at school.

Someone at school or work asks it, half curious, half teasing: how many gods do you have? Ganesha on the dashboard, Krishna in the calendar, Durga at Navratri, Lakshmi at Diwali, a whole shelf at your grandparents' place. It's a fair question, and most people never got a good answer to give. Here's one. First, a guess.
screen: `HOW MANY GODS DO YOU HAVE?` → `A FAIR QUESTION.` → `HERE'S AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: One of the oldest Hindu verses says it in five words: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. That line is how a lot of Hindus answer the question. The many gods are many faces and names of one reality, the way one person can be a mother, a boss and a friend and still be one person. Not every Hindu puts it the same way. Some families give their whole devotion to Vishnu, or Shiva, or the Goddess, and see the others as part of that one. Some honor many, each for a different part of life. Almost everyone has an ishta devata: a chosen deity, the form of God that feels like yours. Often it comes from your family. Sometimes you find your own. So the answer to the question at school can be simple: one truth, many names, and one of them feels like home.
screen: `TRUTH IS ONE.` · `THE WISE CALL IT BY MANY NAMES.` · `MANY FACES, ONE REALITY.` · `THE ONE THAT FEELS LIKE YOURS.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of the image of God you saw most growing up: on a wall, a dashboard, a shelf. Breathe in. As you breathe out, say its name once, quietly, as if it were the name of someone who knows you.
Ishta devata. Your chosen deity: the form of God that feels like yours. Sixth word.
Your line: one truth, many names. Next time someone asks how many gods you have, you've got an answer. Day six.

7.title: not fate, not payback
7.hook: the word everyone borrows, and what it actually says
7.tomorrow: what your grandmother was actually doing
7.howItsDone: Hindu teachers speak of karma as action and its fruit, within this life and across lifetimes; schools of thought differ on how karma works and on how a person is freed from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one truth, many names, and the one that's yours. Six words so far: Ganesha, om, Gayatri, namaste, arti, ishta devata. Today, the seventh.
screen: `GANESHA · OM · GAYATRI · NAMASTE · ARTI · ISHTA DEVATA`

segments.voice: Karma. Someone says it when the car that cut them off gets stopped at the next light. Someone says it when a person who was unkind finally has a bad week. It turns up in song lyrics, on coffee mugs, under photos. Used like that, it means payback: the universe keeping a ledger and settling it on schedule, ideally where you can watch. It's a satisfying idea. It is also not quite what the word means. The older meaning is less about getting even and more about getting made, and it turns the whole thing around to face the one who's using it.
screen: `KARMA.` → `THE CAR AT THE RED LIGHT.` → `PAYBACK?` → `NOT QUITE.`

segments.voice: Karma is the Sanskrit word for action. A deed. Something done. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna points out that no one can stay without acting, even for a moment: breathing, eating, speaking, choosing, all of it is action. So the first thing to know is that karma isn't something that happens to you. It's what you do. The second thing is what action does back. One of the oldest Hindu texts says it like a proverb: as a person acts, so that person becomes. Not: so the person is punished. Becomes. Patience, practiced, turns into a patient person. Sharpness, practiced, turns into a sharp one. A mango seed isn't judged worthy of a mango tree; it grows one because that's what the seed is. The payback version keeps your eyes on other people: did they get what's coming? The older version turns you around: what am I growing with my next word? Hindu teachers also speak of karma across lifetimes, and that's a bigger conversation for later. For today: as you act, so you become.

story.title: the robber's question
story.text: A well-loved telling says the poet Valmiki started out as a robber. One day he tried to rob a wandering sage, who asked him a question: would his family share the weight of what he did? He went home and asked. They said no. What he did was his. Shaken, he changed, and became the poet who would compose the Ramayana.
story.source: a traditional telling of Valmiki's life (later than the Ramayana itself)
